title: NoSQL families and how to choose
scopeHtml: Scope: key-value, document, wide-column and graph stores, CAP and consistency, choosing by access pattern, hot partitions and failure modes.

notes.title: Why NoSQL exists
notes.html:
NoSQL is a family of databases that give up some SQL features (joins, flexible ad-hoc queries, sometimes strict transactions) to get something else: easy horizontal scaling, a flexible schema, or very fast access for one specific pattern.

The honest framing: each NoSQL type is a data structure with a network in front of it. A key-value store is a distributed hash map. A document store is a hash map of JSON. A wide-column store is a sorted map of sorted maps. A graph store is adjacency lists with indexes. If you remember the structure, you can predict what it is good and bad at.

Worked example. One Postgres primary tops out around 10,000 writes/s. A 12-node Cassandra cluster at about 10,000 writes/s per node handles 120,000 writes/s, because each write goes to a few nodes chosen by hashing the key, no single node sees all writes.

Industry examples. Amazon's Dynamo paper (2007) started the wave for the shopping cart; Facebook built Cassandra for inbox search; Google's Bigtable paper inspired HBase; MongoDB took the document route; Neo4j for graphs; Redis for in-memory key-value.

Everyday analogy. A toolbox: a hammer, a screwdriver, a saw. You do not ask which is "best", you ask what you are building.

Common interview traps.

  • Treating NoSQL as "faster SQL". It is faster only for the access pattern it was built around.
  • Saying "NoSQL has no schema". The schema just moves into application code.
  • Forgetting that giving up joins means you design the data around the queries.

notes.title: Key-value stores
notes.html:
A key-value store maps a key to an opaque value. You can get, put and delete by key, and that is nearly all. Because the access path is only the key, the store can hash the key to pick a server, giving near-perfect horizontal scaling and sub-millisecond latency.

Variants: in-memory (Redis, Memcached; microsecond-to-millisecond, limited by RAM) and durable distributed (DynamoDB, Riak, etcd for small coordination data).

# Redis as session store and cache
SET session:8f3a "{\"uid\":42}" EX 1800
GET session:8f3a
INCR rate:42:2026-11-09T10:15     # atomic counter
EXPIRE rate:42:2026-11-09T10:15 60

Worked example. Sessions: 10M active x 1 KB = 10 GB. One Redis node with 32 GB RAM holds it; a single node does about 100,000 ops/s. If you need 1M ops/s, use Redis Cluster with 16,384 hash slots spread over, say, 10 primaries.

Best for: sessions, caches, rate limiters, feature flags, shopping carts, leaderboards (sorted sets), idempotency keys. Bad for: range queries over values, reporting, relationships.

Industry examples. Twitter and Instagram cache heavily in Memcached/Redis. DynamoDB powers Amazon's cart and many AWS-backed apps (single-digit millisecond at any scale, pay by capacity). Discord used Redis and Cassandra/ScyllaDB.

Everyday analogy. A cloakroom: hand over a numbered ticket, get your coat instantly. You cannot ask "give me all red coats".

Common interview traps.

  • Using Redis as the only copy of important data without persistence (RDB/AOF) and replicas.
  • Huge values (multi-MB) or giant keys (a 5 GB sorted set) that block the single-threaded event loop.
  • Cache stampede when a hot key expires (use jitter, locking or request coalescing).

notes.title: Document stores
notes.html:
A document store keeps self-contained JSON-like documents, usually grouped in collections, and lets you query inside them. One document holds everything for an entity, so one read gets all of it with no join.

{
  "_id": "order_981",
  "customerId": 42,
  "status": "PAID",
  "items": [
    {"sku": "A1", "qty": 2, "priceCents": 4900},
    {"sku": "B7", "qty": 1, "priceCents": 1500}
  ],
  "shipTo": {"city": "Pune", "pin": "411001"}
}

The central design choice is embed vs reference. Embed data read together (items inside the order). Reference data that is large, shared, or changes independently (the product catalogue). Documents have size limits (MongoDB: 16 MB), so never embed an unbounded list (all comments of a viral post).

Worked example. Product page: product + 20 reviews + seller info. Embedding top 20 reviews in the product document gives one 3 KB read at about 1 ms. Storing all 50,000 reviews separately and referencing them by productId avoids the unbounded-array problem.

Scaling. MongoDB shards by a shard key (hashed or ranged) across replica sets. A poor shard key, such as a monotonically increasing timestamp, sends all inserts to one shard (hot shard).

Best for: catalogues, content management, user profiles with variable attributes, event payloads. Bad for: many-to-many relationships and heavy multi-document transactions (supported in modern MongoDB but slower and costlier).

Industry examples. eBay, Forbes and many e-commerce catalogues use MongoDB. Firestore and DynamoDB (document-ish) power mobile backends; Couchbase is popular in travel and retail.

Everyday analogy. A folder per customer with every paper about them inside, instead of one drawer per type of paper across all customers.

Common interview traps.

  • Embedding unbounded arrays until the document hits the size cap or becomes slow to rewrite.
  • Picking a monotonically increasing shard key.
  • Recreating relational joins by hand with many round trips.

notes.title: Wide-column stores
notes.html:
A wide-column store is a sorted map: partition key picks the server, clustering columns sort the rows inside that partition. Cassandra, ScyllaDB, HBase and Bigtable work like this. Writes are very fast (an append to a log plus memory, see the LSM note), and the cluster has no single leader in Cassandra's case.

You design the table for one query. The rule: "model tables around queries, not entities".

-- Cassandra CQL: messages in a chat, newest first within a conversation
CREATE TABLE messages_by_conversation (
  conversation_id uuid,
  bucket          int,          -- e.g. day number, bounds partition size
  sent_at         timeuuid,
  sender_id       bigint,
  body            text,
  PRIMARY KEY ((conversation_id, bucket), sent_at)
) WITH CLUSTERING ORDER BY (sent_at DESC);

Partition key (conversation_id, bucket) decides the node; sent_at sorts rows inside it. Keep partitions under roughly 100 MB / 100k rows; add a bucket to a huge conversation so it does not become a hot, giant partition.

Tunable consistency. With replication factor N=3, writes at QUORUM (2) and reads at QUORUM (2) overlap (R + W > N), giving strong-ish consistency; ONE is faster but may read stale data.

Worked example. Discord stored trillions of messages; they moved from Cassandra to ScyllaDB because of GC pauses and hot partitions on busy channels (their public blog). Netflix uses Cassandra for viewing history with multi-region replication; Apple reportedly runs very large Cassandra fleets.

Best for: write-heavy time-series, message history, activity feeds, IoT, anything keyed by "give me the latest N for X". Bad for: ad-hoc queries, joins, secondary indexes on high-cardinality columns, frequent deletes (tombstones).

Decision gravity. Partition key choice is a one-way door; changing it means rewriting the table.

Everyday analogy. A filing cabinet where each drawer (partition) is on a different floor, and inside a drawer, papers are always sorted by date.

Common interview traps.

  • Unbounded partitions (one partition per user that grows forever).
  • Querying without the partition key (needs ALLOW FILTERING, a full scan).
  • Using Cassandra like a queue: delete-heavy workloads create tombstones that slow reads.

notes.title: Graph databases
notes.html:
A graph database stores nodes (things) and edges (relationships) and makes walking relationships cheap. In SQL a "friends of friends of friends" query needs a self-join per hop, and cost grows quickly. In a native graph store (Neo4j), each node points directly to its neighbours ("index-free adjacency"), so a hop costs roughly the number of neighbours, not the table size.

// Cypher (Neo4j): people who follow someone I follow, but I do not follow
MATCH (me:User {id: 42})-[:FOLLOWS]->(:User)-[:FOLLOWS]->(rec:User)
WHERE NOT (me)-[:FOLLOWS]->(rec)
RETURN rec.id, count(*) AS mutuals
ORDER BY mutuals DESC LIMIT 10

Worked example. 1M users, average 200 follows. Depth 2 = 200 x 200 = 40,000 paths; depth 3 = 8M. That blow-up (super-nodes with millions of followers) is why graph systems need limits, sampling or precomputation.

Scaling reality. Graphs are hard to shard because edges cross any partition. Many large companies use a custom store: Facebook's TAO is a graph-shaped cache over sharded MySQL; Pinterest and Twitter built purpose-made graph services (FlockDB). Neo4j scales reads with replicas and has sharding in newer versions (confirm in docs).

Best for: fraud rings, recommendations, knowledge graphs, access-control hierarchies, network topology. Bad for: bulk analytics scans and simple key lookups.

Everyday analogy. A subway map: the question "how do I get from A to B" is natural. Answering it from a list of stations in a spreadsheet is painful.

Common interview traps.

  • Using a graph DB when SQL with a recursive CTE and 2 hops would do.
  • Ignoring super-nodes (celebrities) that make traversals explode.
  • Assuming a graph DB shards as easily as a key-value store.

notes.title: CAP, consistency and what you give up
notes.html:
CAP says that during a network partition a distributed store must choose between consistency (everyone sees the latest write) and availability (every request gets an answer). Outside partitions, the real daily trade-off is latency vs consistency (PACELC).

Store Typical stance Notes
Cassandra, DynamoDB (default), Riak AP, tunable Eventual consistency, conflict resolution by last-write-wins or vectors
MongoDB (replica set) CP-leaning Writes go to primary; reads from secondaries may lag
HBase, Bigtable, Spanner, etcd CP Strong consistency, may reject during partitions
Redis (async replicas) Fast, may lose last writes on failover Use WAIT or avoid for critical data

Worked example. Cassandra N=3. Write at ONE then read at ONE: a read could hit the replica that has not yet got the write, a stale read for milliseconds to seconds. Writes at QUORUM and reads at QUORUM: R+W=4 > 3, so the read set always overlaps the latest write.

Industry examples. Amazon's cart tolerated merging duplicate items (shopping cart "add always wins") instead of losing an add. Spanner uses atomic clocks (TrueTime) to give strong consistency across the globe at higher write latency (commit waits of roughly 7 to 10 ms is a commonly quoted order of magnitude).

Everyday analogy. Two bank branches whose phone line is cut: either both refuse to give cash (consistent, unavailable) or both keep serving using last known balance (available, risk of overdraft).

Common interview traps.

  • Saying "CAP: pick two". Partitions happen; the choice is C or A during one.
  • Calling eventual consistency "broken". It is fine for likes, wrong for balances.
  • Forgetting read-your-writes and monotonic reads, which users notice immediately.

notes.title: How to choose
notes.html:
Start from the access pattern, not the product name. Ask in this order:

  1. What are the top 3 queries, and their QPS and latency target?
  2. Do I need multi-row transactions or joins?
  3. How big will it be in 1 and 3 years, and what is the write rate?
  4. How much staleness can the business tolerate?
  5. What does the team already operate well?
Requirement Pick
Money, inventory, bookings SQL
Cache, session, counter, rate limit Redis / Memcached
Flexible-schema catalogue, content Document (MongoDB, Firestore)
Millions of writes/s, time-ordered per key Wide-column (Cassandra, Scylla, Bigtable)
Fraud rings, recommendations Graph
Full-text and filters Search engine (Elasticsearch, OpenSearch)
Serverless key-value with zero ops DynamoDB

Polyglot persistence means using several stores, each as a specialist, with one system of record and others derived (cache, search index, analytics) fed by events or CDC (change data capture, e.g. Debezium). More stores mean more ways for copies to drift and more things to operate.

Decision gravity. The system of record is a one-way door. Derived stores (cache, search, graph projection) are reversible: rebuild from the source.

Worked example. A ride-hailing app: trips and payments in SQL (correctness), driver location in Redis geo (hot, ephemeral, 100k updates/s), trip history in Cassandra (append-heavy), search of places in Elasticsearch. Uber and Lyft are known to run mixes like this.

Everyday analogy. A kitchen: fridge for fresh, freezer for long-term, pantry for dry goods. Putting everything in the freezer works, but badly.

Common interview traps.

  • Choosing by hype or resume.
  • Using five stores for a 2,000-user app.
  • Not naming the source of truth when several stores hold the same data.

notes.title: Production patterns and failure modes
notes.html:
Hot partitions. One key gets most of the traffic (a celebrity, a viral product). Symptom: one node at 100 percent CPU, others idle; DynamoDB shows ThrottlingException despite spare table capacity. Fixes: key salting (key#0..N), caching, splitting the key by time bucket.

Tombstones and compaction debt (Cassandra). Deletes write markers that linger until compaction; reads scan them. Symptom: read latency creeps up on a delete-heavy table; the warning "Read X live rows and Y tombstone cells" appears in logs.

Large documents. A document growing from 5 KB to 8 MB means each update rewrites a lot. Metric: rising write latency and oplog size.

Unbounded fan-out. A graph or follow list with a 50M-follower node. Fix by limiting, sampling or precomputing.

Capacity planning for DynamoDB (example). 1 write capacity unit = one write of up to 1 KB per second; 1 read capacity unit = one strongly consistent read of up to 4 KB per second. 5,000 writes/s of 2 KB items = 10,000 WCU. On-demand mode avoids planning but costs more at steady load.

Industry examples. Instagram's "Justin Bieber problem" is the classic hot-key example. Many teams report DynamoDB throttling from a single hot partition key.

Everyday analogy. One checkout lane with a queue of 100 while seven other lanes are empty.

Common interview traps.

  • Designing a key without asking "which key will be hottest?".
  • Not testing with real data skew (80/20 or worse).
  • Forgetting backups and restore testing for NoSQL stores.

notes.title: Summary
notes.html:
• NoSQL types are data structures: key-value (hash map), document (JSON), wide-column (sorted map), graph (nodes/edges). Each wins only for its access pattern.
  • Key-value: fastest and simplest, lookup by key only. Document: embed what you read together, reference the rest, avoid unbounded arrays.
  • Wide-column: model one table per query; partition key = placement, clustering key = order; bound partition size.
  • Graph: great for multi-hop relationships; sharding and super-nodes are the pain.
  • CAP: during a partition choose C or A; day to day it is latency vs consistency; quorum R+W>N gives overlap.
  • Choose from the top queries, transaction needs, size and staleness tolerance. Keep one system of record; derived stores are rebuildable.
  • Watch for hot partitions, tombstones, huge documents and super-nodes.

questions.promptHtml: What are the main NoSQL families and what is each one good at?

sections.label: Why interviewers ask this
sections.html: A baseline check that you map each store to a data structure and an access pattern, not a brand name.

sections.label: 30-second answer
sections.html: Each is a data structure with a network in front. Key-value (Redis, DynamoDB) is a distributed hash map: fast lookup by key only. Document (MongoDB, Firestore) is a map of JSON documents: one read returns a whole entity. Wide-column (Cassandra, Bigtable) is a sorted map of sorted maps: huge write rates, queries by partition key. Graph (Neo4j) is nodes and edges: cheap multi-hop traversals. They trade joins and ad-hoc queries for scale or a flexible shape, so you design data around queries.

sections.label: Deep explanation
sections.html:
Key-value   -> hash map            get/put by key
Document    -> JSON blobs          query inside, embed or reference
Wide-column -> partition + sorted  one table per query
Graph       -> nodes and edges     walk relationships

Why scale is easy: the key is hashed to pick a node, so no single machine sees all writes. Example: one Postgres primary at about 10,000 writes/s vs a 12-node Cassandra cluster at about 10,000 writes/s per node = 120,000 writes/s.

"No schema" is false: the schema moves into application code. "NoSQL is faster" is false: it is faster for the pattern it was built for.

sections.label: Common mistakes & traps
sections.html:
• Treating NoSQL as faster SQL.
  • Forgetting that without joins, the data model follows the queries.
  • Choosing by hype or resume.

sections.label: Follow-ups
sections.html:
1. Which for sessions? -> Key-value with TTL (Redis).
  2. Which for a product catalogue with variable attributes? -> Document.
  3. Which for chat history by conversation? -> Wide-column.

sections.label: 3-YOE vs senior answer
sections.html: Average: lists names. Senior: ties each to a structure, states what it cannot do, and starts from the top three queries.

sections.label: Production connection
sections.html: A team picked a document store for relational reporting data and spent months replicating joins in code.

questions.promptHtml: In a document database, how do you decide between embedding and referencing related data?

sections.label: Why interviewers ask this
sections.html: The central modeling decision in document stores; bad choices cause oversized documents or N+1 round trips.

sections.label: 30-second answer
sections.html: I embed data that is read together and bounded in size, like order line items inside the order, so one read returns everything. I reference data that is large, shared, unbounded or changes independently, like the product catalogue or all reviews of a viral product. Documents have size limits (MongoDB 16 MB) and every update rewrites more as a document grows, so I never embed an unbounded list.

sections.label: Deep explanation
sections.html:
{
  "_id": "order_981", "customerId": 42, "status": "PAID",
  "items": [ {"sku": "A1", "qty": 2, "priceCents": 4900} ],
  "shipTo": {"city": "Pune", "pin": "411001"}
}

Worked example: a product page needs product, top 20 reviews, seller info. Embed the top 20 reviews (a 3 KB read, about 1 ms) and keep the remaining 50,000 reviews in a separate collection keyed by productId. Copy a snapshot of price into the order line (the order must remember the price paid) while referencing the live catalogue for display.

Heuristics: one-to-few embed; one-to-many reference; many-to-many reference. Multi-document transactions exist in modern MongoDB but cost more.

sections.label: Common mistakes & traps
sections.html:
• Unbounded arrays until the size cap.
  • Recreating joins by hand with many round trips.
  • Monotonically increasing shard key (sends all inserts to one shard).

sections.label: Follow-ups
sections.html:
1. What if seller name changes? -> If embedded, update many documents or accept stale copies; reference when it must be current.
  2. Shard key choice? -> Hashed or high-cardinality key matching the main query; not a timestamp.
  3. When is SQL better? -> Many-to-many relations and multi-entity transactions.

sections.label: 3-YOE vs senior answer
sections.html: Average: "embed for speed". Senior: bounds, update frequency, snapshot vs live reference, size caps, shard key interaction.

sections.label: Production connection
sections.html: A comments array embedded in a post grew to 6 MB; each new comment rewrote the document and write latency climbed.

questions.contextHtml:
You model chat history on Cassandra: "show the latest 50 messages of a conversation, newest first". First attempt:

CREATE TABLE messages (
  conversation_id uuid,
  sent_at timeuuid,
  sender_id bigint,
  body text,
  PRIMARY KEY (conversation_id, sent_at)
) WITH CLUSTERING ORDER BY (sent_at DESC);

Six months in, one company-wide channel has 40M messages; queries on it time out. nodetool tablehistograms shows partition size max 38 GB and p99 read latency 2.1 s for that channel; other conversations are fine at 4 ms.
questions.promptHtml: What is wrong and how do you change the model?

sections.label: What a weak answer looks like
sections.html: "Add more nodes." One partition lives on one replica set; more nodes do not split it.

sections.label: Strong answer
sections.html:
1. Clarifying questions I'd ask: How do clients read: latest N, or deep history? Max message rate per channel? Is retention bounded?
  2. Immediate mitigation: Cache the latest 50 for that channel in Redis; lower read consistency to LOCAL_QUORUM if it is ALL.
  3. Hypotheses, ranked: Unbounded partition (conversation_id alone); partition above roughly 100 MB or 100k rows is a red flag; a hot partition on busy channels; compaction pressure on huge partitions.
  4. How I'd verify: nodetool tablehistograms, nodetool tablestats for max partition bytes, trace one slow query.
  5. Root cause: The partition key does not bound partition size.
  6. Fix: Add a time bucket to the partition key.
CREATE TABLE messages_by_conversation (
  conversation_id uuid, bucket int,       -- e.g. days since epoch
  sent_at timeuuid, sender_id bigint, body text,
  PRIMARY KEY ((conversation_id, bucket), sent_at)
) WITH CLUSTERING ORDER BY (sent_at DESC);

Read the newest bucket first, walk back one bucket if fewer than 50 rows. Migrate: dual write, backfill buckets, cut over reads. For very hot channels use smaller buckets (hourly). 7. Prevention: Alert on max partition size; add skewed channels to load tests. 8. Trade-offs & what I'd NOT do: Bucketing makes cross-bucket queries multi-read. The partition key is a one-way door; changing it means rewriting the table. Not ALLOW FILTERING.

sections.label: Curveball follow-ups
sections.html:
• Query "all messages by sender"? -> Another table keyed by sender_id (denormalise per query).
  • Deletes of old messages? -> Use TTL and time-window compaction to avoid tombstone pain.

sections.label: Senior war story
sections.html: The company-wide channel was the only partition that ever mattered; adding a day bucket cut p99 from seconds to milliseconds.

sections.label: Scoring rubric
sections.html:
• No hire: Add nodes.
  • Hire: Bucketed partition key.
  • Strong hire: Size thresholds, dual-write migration, per-query tables, TTL/compaction.

questions.contextHtml:
Redis (single primary, 3 replicas) backs sessions and a leaderboard. Every day at 18:00 API latency spikes for 4 to 6 seconds across all services. Metrics:

slowlog: ZRANGE leaderboard:global 0 -1 WITHSCORES  duration 3,840,000 us
slowlog: KEYS session:*                              duration 1,210,000 us
used_memory 21 GB ; leaderboard:global = 4.8 GB (sorted set, 31M members)
connected_clients 4,200 ; blocked on single thread; CPU 100% on one core

Nothing else changed; the 18:00 job is a "weekly report" cron.

sections.label: What a weak answer looks like
sections.html: "Redis is slow; add a replica." Reads of that key and KEYS still hit one thread.

sections.label: Strong answer
sections.html:
1. Clarifying questions I'd ask: Who runs the 18:00 job? Is it hitting the primary? Do we need the full set or only top N?
  2. Immediate mitigation: Disable or reroute the cron; CONFIG SET rename or block KEYS via ACL; kill the long command if needed.
  3. Hypotheses, ranked: ZRANGE 0 -1 over 31M members and KEYS * are O(N) commands blocking the single-threaded event loop; a giant key; memory not the problem.
  4. How I'd verify: SLOWLOG GET, redis-cli --bigkeys, MEMORY USAGE leaderboard:global.
  5. Root cause: O(N) commands on a huge key stall every client, because commands are executed on one thread.
  6. Fix: Use ZRANGE 0 99 (top N) or ZSCAN; replace KEYS with SCAN and cursor; split the leaderboard (per region or time bucket); run reports on a replica or an analytic copy; add ACLs to deny KEYS.
  7. Prevention: slowlog-log-slower-than alerts, command allow-list, big-key scan in CI, client timeouts.
  8. Trade-offs & what I'd NOT do: Replica reads can be stale; fine for reports. UNLINK instead of DEL for deleting large keys (non-blocking).

sections.label: Curveball follow-ups
sections.html:
• Sessions are the only copy; Redis restarts? -> Enable AOF or RDB plus replica, or accept re-login; decide explicitly.
  • Cache stampede on expiry? -> Jitter TTLs, request coalescing.

sections.label: Senior war story
sections.html: A single HGETALL on a 200 MB hash by a debugging script froze production for 3 seconds every time it was run.

sections.label: Scoring rubric
sections.html:
• No hire: Add replicas or memory.
  • Hire: Identifies O(N) on big key, uses SCAN and top N.
  • Strong hire: ACLs, UNLINK, replica for reports, persistence stance.

questions.contextHtml:
A forum stores each thread as a MongoDB document and shards the threads collection on { createdAt: 1 }:

{
  "_id": "t_77",
  "title": "Launch day",
  "createdAt": "2026-11-09T10:15:00Z",
  "posts": [ {"user": "u1", "text": "...", "at": "..."} ]
}

After a viral thread: update latency for it goes 4 ms to 900 ms, and writes errors appear: BSONObj size: 16793600 is invalid. Sharding stats show one shard taking 100% of inserts; the other 3 shards idle.
questions.promptHtml: Find the design bugs and fix them.

sections.label: What a weak answer looks like
sections.html: "Increase the document limit" (it is a hard 16 MB cap) or "add shards".

sections.label: Strong answer
sections.html:
1. Clarifying questions I'd ask: Is posts queried by thread, by user, or both? How many posts can a thread have? What are the main read patterns (latest page of posts)?
  2. Immediate mitigation: Cap thread size operationally (lock the thread or move extra posts into an overflow collection).
  3. Hypotheses, ranked: Unbounded embedded array hits 16 MB and each update rewrites a large document; the shard key createdAt is monotonically increasing so all inserts hit the max-chunk shard.
  4. How I'd verify: db.threads.stats(), sh.status() chunk distribution, per-shard op counters.
  5. Root cause: Wrong embed choice for an unbounded list; monotonic shard key.
  6. Fix: Move posts to their own collection {threadId, seq, user, text, at} with an index on (threadId, seq); keep a small summary (counts, last post) in the thread. Shard the posts collection on a hashed threadId (or compound {threadId: 1, seq: 1} if range queries by thread dominate and a single thread cannot become too hot); shard threads on hashed _id.
  7. Prevention: Design review rule: "no unbounded arrays"; test with skewed (viral) data.
  8. Trade-offs & what I'd NOT do: Referencing costs a second query for the latest page, which is acceptable; a hashed key loses range scans across threads. Shard key changes are painful (resharding exists in newer versions; verify for your version).

sections.label: Curveball follow-ups
sections.html:
• A single viral thread is still hot after hashing? -> Hash on {threadId, seq bucket} or cache the latest page.
  • Need transactions across thread and post? -> Avoid; use idempotent writes and counters updated asynchronously.

sections.label: Senior war story
sections.html: A team discovered the 16 MB limit in production on the biggest thread of the year, the worst possible day.

sections.label: Scoring rubric
sections.html:
• No hire: Add shards or raise limits.
  • Hire: Splits posts, fixes shard key.
  • Strong hire: Compound keys, hot thread handling, skewed test data.

questions.contextHtml:
Cassandra, RF=3, one datacenter. An inventory-like counter "seats left" is written and read at consistency ONE for speed. Users occasionally see seats available when a show is sold out; two buyers got the same last seat. Metrics:

write CL=ONE, read CL=ONE
read repair: 3.1% of reads trigger repair
hint backlog on node-5: 2.4M hints (node-5 was down 40 min last night)
nodetool status: all UN now

The team asks whether to "just use QUORUM".

sections.label: What a weak answer looks like
sections.html: "QUORUM fixes it" without explaining why, or "Cassandra is broken".

sections.label: Strong answer
sections.html:
1. Clarifying questions I'd ask: Is "seats left" a hard invariant? Do we need compare-and-set? Is the write path idempotent?
  2. Immediate mitigation: Hold ticket sales for that show or route purchases through a single serialized path; raise to QUORUM for reads and writes on this table.
  3. Hypotheses, ranked: CL=ONE reads may hit a replica that missed the write (node-5 recovering from hints); concurrent buyers read the same value and both write (lost update, not just staleness).
  4. How I'd verify: Check replica values with SELECT at different CLs, nodetool hints, timing between writes.
  5. Root cause: R + W = 2 is not greater than N = 3, so reads can miss the latest write; and read-modify-write without atomicity is a race regardless of consistency level.
  6. Fix: QUORUM/QUORUM gives R + W = 4 > 3 so read sets overlap the latest write. But it still does not make "read seat count then decrement" safe. For a hard invariant use a lightweight transaction (UPDATE ... IF seats > 0, Paxos-based, slower), or a single-writer per show via a queue, or keep inventory in SQL.
UPDATE show_seats SET holder = :user WHERE show_id = :s AND seat = :n IF holder = null;
  1. Prevention: Per-table consistency policy in code review; test with concurrent buyers.
  2. Trade-offs & what I'd NOT do: QUORUM raises latency and lowers availability when 2 nodes are down. Eventual consistency is fine for likes, wrong for stock.

sections.label: Curveball follow-ups
sections.html:
• One datacenter down in a two-DC cluster? -> LOCAL_QUORUM per DC keeps latency local but cross-DC conflicts need design.
  • Why not just SQL? -> Often the right answer for bookings; keep Cassandra for the append-heavy history.

sections.label: Senior war story
sections.html: Double-booked seats at launch traced to CL=ONE on a "temporary" test setting that shipped.

sections.label: Scoring rubric
sections.html:
• No hire: "Use QUORUM" with no reasoning.
  • Hire: R+W>N reasoning and notes the race.
  • Strong hire: LWT or single-writer, SQL for the invariant, per-table CL policy.

questions.promptHtml: Explain CAP correctly, and how quorum reads and writes give consistency in a replicated store.

sections.label: Why interviewers ask this
sections.html: "Pick two of three" is a common wrong answer; the interviewer wants the partition-time choice and the everyday latency trade-off.

sections.label: 30-second answer
sections.html: CAP says that during a network partition a distributed store must choose consistency (everyone sees the latest write, some requests may be refused) or availability (every request answers, possibly with stale data). Partitions happen, so the real choice is C or A while one is happening; day to day the trade is latency versus consistency (PACELC). With N replicas, writing to W and reading from R replicas with R + W > N makes the read set overlap the latest write.

sections.label: Deep explanation
sections.html:
Store Typical stance
Cassandra, DynamoDB default, Riak AP, tunable, eventual
MongoDB replica set CP-leaning (writes to primary; secondary reads may lag)
HBase, Bigtable, Spanner, etcd CP
Redis with async replicas Fast, can lose last writes on failover

Quorum, N=3: write QUORUM (2) + read QUORUM (2) = 4 > 3, so a read always includes at least one replica with the latest acknowledged write. Write ONE + read ONE = 2, no overlap, stale reads possible for ms to seconds. Spanner gets global strong consistency using TrueTime, paying commit wait (order of 7 to 10 ms, verify).

Users notice read-your-writes and monotonic reads violations immediately; eventual consistency is fine for likes, wrong for balances. Amazon's cart merged duplicate adds instead of losing an add.

sections.label: Common mistakes & traps
sections.html:
• "CAP: pick two."
  • Calling eventual consistency broken.
  • Assuming quorum gives transactions (it does not give atomic read-modify-write).

sections.label: Follow-ups
sections.html:
1. W=ALL for strong reads? -> Any node failure blocks writes; availability cost.
  2. Conflicts in AP stores? -> Last-write-wins (clock-dependent, can lose writes) or vector clocks/CRDTs.
  3. Where does latency come in? -> Waiting for more replicas, or cross-region acks.

sections.label: 3-YOE vs senior answer
sections.html: Average: recites CAP. Senior: partition-time vs normal-time trade, quorum arithmetic, per-operation consistency choices.

sections.label: Production connection
sections.html: An AP store with last-write-wins and skewed clocks silently kept the older of two profile updates.

questions.promptHtml: How do you choose a datastore for a new feature, and when is using several stores justified?

sections.label: Why interviewers ask this
sections.html: Tests a repeatable method rather than product preference, plus awareness of the cost of polyglot persistence.

sections.label: 30-second answer
sections.html: I start from the top three queries with their QPS and latency, then ask about multi-row transactions or joins, size and write rate in one and three years, staleness the business tolerates, and what the team already runs well. Money and stock go to SQL; cache, sessions and counters to Redis; flexible catalogues to a document store; huge keyed write streams to wide-column; deep relationships to a graph; text search to a search engine. If I use several stores I name one system of record and treat the rest as derived and rebuildable.

sections.label: Deep explanation
sections.html:
System of record (SQL) --CDC/events--> cache | search index | analytics | graph projection

Ride-hailing example: trips and payments in SQL, driver location in Redis geo (100k updates/s, ephemeral), trip history in a wide-column store, place search in Elasticsearch.

Costs of polyglot: more things to operate, more drift between copies, harder debugging, more failure modes. A 2,000-user app should not run five stores. Decision gravity: the system of record is a one-way door; derived stores are two-way because you can rebuild them.

Derived data needs a sync path: CDC (Debezium) or the outbox pattern, plus reconciliation.

sections.label: Common mistakes & traps
sections.html:
• Choosing by hype or resume.
  • No named source of truth when several stores hold the same data.
  • Not asking which key will be hottest, or testing with uniform data.

sections.label: Follow-ups
sections.html:
1. How do you keep search in sync? -> CDC from the primary; idempotent index updates; periodic full reindex.
  2. When add Redis? -> When a measured read pattern needs microsecond keyed access; cache is derived.
  3. Backups across stores? -> Restore the system of record; rebuild derived ones; test restores.

sections.label: 3-YOE vs senior answer
sections.html: Average: "right tool for the job". Senior: a decision procedure, one-way vs two-way doors, operational cost, drift control.

sections.label: Production connection
sections.html: Three services each kept a "copy" of customer data in different stores; after an outage nobody knew which was correct.

questions.contextHtml:
A flash-sale app stores product stock counters in DynamoDB, table keyed by productId. Provisioned: 40,000 WCU. During a sale on one product:

ConsumedWriteCapacityUnits (table): 11,000 / 40,000 (27%)
ThrottledRequests: 9,400/s on PutItem/UpdateItem
ThrottlingException: Rate of requests exceeds the allowed throughput
hot key: productId=P-8812 receiving ~6,000 writes/s

Other products succeed. Finance asks why throttling happens when "we have 73% capacity free".

sections.label: What a weak answer looks like
sections.html: "Raise provisioned capacity to 100,000."

sections.label: Strong answer
sections.html:
1. Clarifying questions I'd ask: Must the stock be exact? Is it a decrement per purchase? Are reads also hot (the product page)?
  2. Immediate mitigation: Cache reads (DAX or Redis); queue purchase requests for that product to smooth writes; throttle checkout via a waiting room.
  3. Hypotheses, ranked: One partition can absorb only a fixed throughput (about 1,000 WCU per partition, verify current limits); a single item key concentrates all writes in one partition; adaptive capacity helps but cannot split one key.
  4. How I'd verify: CloudWatch Contributor Insights for the most-accessed keys.
  5. Root cause: Hot key; the table-level capacity is not the limit, the per-partition limit is.
  6. Fix: Shard the counter: productId#0..N items with the stock allocated across them; purchases pick a shard at random (or by user hash), and a shard with 0 stock retries another; sum shards for display. Alternatively reserve stock in a queue with one consumer per product.
P-8812#0 -> partition A
P-8812#1 -> partition B
P-8812#2 -> partition C

For exact stock use conditional writes (ConditionExpression: stock >= 1) on the shard. 7. Prevention: Load test with real skew; alerts on throttled requests per key; salt planning in the data model review. 8. Trade-offs & what I'd NOT do: Sharded stock makes "last item" allocation fiddly (rebalance shards); on-demand mode raises cost and still has per-partition limits. Capacity bump does not help a single key.

sections.label: Curveball follow-ups
sections.html:
• Read-hot product page? -> DAX or CDN caching.
  • Exactness required? -> A relational row with SELECT ... FOR UPDATE serialized per product may be better at this volume.

sections.label: Senior war story
sections.html: A team doubled capacity twice during a sale and saw zero improvement until someone read the hot-key report.

sections.label: Scoring rubric
sections.html:
• No hire: Increase capacity.
  • Hire: Hot key explanation and key salting.
  • Strong hire: Conditional writes, queue/waiting room, caching, exactness trade-off.

questions.contextHtml:
A team uses Cassandra as a job queue: insert a row into pending_jobs partitioned by queue_name, workers read the first 100 rows and delete each after processing. After 3 weeks, p99 read latency goes 5 ms to 4 s and workers time out. Logs:

WARN ReadCommand: Read 100 live rows and 1,874,332 tombstone cells for query SELECT * FROM pending_jobs WHERE queue_name='emails' LIMIT 100
tombstone_failure_threshold: 100000 (aborts query)

Compaction is running; gc_grace_seconds is the default 10 days. Disk is at 55%.

sections.label: What a weak answer looks like
sections.html: "Run a repair" or "add nodes".

sections.label: Strong answer
sections.html:
1. Clarifying questions I'd ask: Throughput of jobs? Do we need ordering? Is there a delay/retry requirement?
  2. Immediate mitigation: Pause producers briefly; reduce gc_grace_seconds on this table carefully (only if repairs run within that window) and force compaction; or temporarily move the queue name to a new partition bucket.
  3. Hypotheses, ranked: Delete-heavy queue pattern leaves tombstones until gc_grace_seconds passes and compaction removes them; reads scan the whole tombstone range before reaching live rows; unbounded partition.
  4. How I'd verify: nodetool tablestats for tombstone-per-slice metrics, trace the query, warnings in logs.
  5. Root cause: Cassandra is an LSM; deletes write markers, not remove data; a queue turns every row into a tombstone.
  6. Fix: Use a real queue (Kafka, SQS, RabbitMQ) or SQL with FOR UPDATE SKIP LOCKED for job claiming. If it must stay in Cassandra: time-bucketed partitions (queue_name, hour) so old partitions can be dropped or TTL-expired by time-window compaction, and read only recent buckets.
  7. Prevention: Design rule "no queues or delete-heavy workloads in Cassandra"; alert on tombstone warnings.
  8. Trade-offs & what I'd NOT do: Lowering gc_grace_seconds risks resurrecting deleted data if a replica was down longer and repair did not run. Not raise tombstone_failure_threshold (hides the problem).

sections.label: Curveball follow-ups
sections.html:
• Why does the queue pattern look OK at first? -> Tombstones accumulate over days; early reads are fast.
  • Use TTL instead of DELETE? -> TTL also creates tombstones when it expires; time-window compaction helps by dropping whole files.

sections.label: Senior war story
sections.html: A scheduled-jobs table looked healthy for 3 weeks, then degraded all at once as gc_grace windows rolled over.

sections.label: Scoring rubric
sections.html:
• No hire: Repair or add nodes.
  • Hire: Names tombstones, moves to a queue or buckets.
  • Strong hire: gc_grace risk, TWCS, SKIP LOCKED alternative, alerts.

questions.contextHtml:
A social app wants "people you may know": friends of friends ranked by mutual friends. 20M users, average 150 follows, some celebrities with 30M followers. The SQL prototype:

SELECT f2.followee_id, count(*) AS mutuals
FROM follows f1 JOIN follows f2 ON f2.follower_id = f1.followee_id
WHERE f1.follower_id = :me AND f2.followee_id <> :me
GROUP BY 1 ORDER BY mutuals DESC LIMIT 10;

It takes 40 ms for typical users but 11 s for users who follow a celebrity. Depth-2 expansion: 150 x 150 = 22,500 paths normally. A proposal: "move to Neo4j".
questions.promptHtml: Do you move to a graph database? What do you do?

sections.label: What a weak answer looks like
sections.html: "Yes, graphs are made for this" without addressing super-nodes or sharding.

sections.label: Strong answer
sections.html:
1. Clarifying questions I'd ask: Must recommendations be real time or can they be precomputed daily? Depth only 2? Freshness needed? Do we already have the follow graph elsewhere?
  2. Immediate mitigation: Cap fan-out: skip nodes with more than, say, 5,000 followers in the expansion, or sample.
  3. Hypotheses, ranked: The slow cases are celebrities (the expansion hits 30M edges), which a graph DB also struggles with; typical users are fine in SQL; depth 2 with an index is within SQL's reach.
  4. How I'd verify: EXPLAIN ANALYZE showing rows per join, distribution of followee counts.
  5. Root cause: Super-node explosion, not the storage engine.
  6. Fix: Precompute recommendations offline (batch job over the follow edges, e.g. nightly) and serve from a key-value table recs:{user}; for freshness add an incremental job for new follows. Skip or sample super-nodes. Consider a graph DB only if the product needs many hops, ad-hoc pattern queries (fraud rings), or depth 3+ at interactive latency, and plan how it shards (edges cross partitions; Facebook's TAO is graph-shaped over sharded MySQL).
  7. Prevention: Test with skewed degrees (power law), limit traversal cost with a budget per query.
  8. Trade-offs & what I'd NOT do: Another store means CDC sync and operations; precomputed recs go stale by hours, acceptable for this feature. Depth 3 here is 8M paths per user: never online.

sections.label: Curveball follow-ups
sections.html:
• Fraud ring detection, 6 hops, ad hoc? -> That is the graph DB case.
  • Graph DB sharding? -> Hard; many run replicas for reads and keep the graph within one machine's memory (check current vendor support).

sections.label: Senior war story
sections.html: The expensive users were not the average ones but the few with celebrity connections; sampling super-nodes cut p99 from seconds to 60 ms without a new database.

sections.label: Scoring rubric
sections.html:
• No hire: Moves to graph DB, ignores super-nodes.
  • Hire: Identifies super-nodes, precompute or cap.
  • Strong hire: States when a graph DB is justified, sharding limits, skewed-data testing.

questions.contextHtml:
Post-incident review of a retailer. Stores: Postgres (orders), Elasticsearch (product search), Redis (cart and prices cache), and MongoDB (product details, added by a different team). On a sale day customers were charged 499 for products shown at 399 in search; 2,300 orders were affected. Findings:

Postgres price: 499   (updated 09:58 by pricing service)
MongoDB price:  399   (updated by CMS import at 09:40, never overwritten)
Elasticsearch:  399   (indexed from MongoDB)
Redis price:    499   (TTL 24h, from Postgres at 09:59)
no job compares the stores; the "price" field exists in 4 places
questions.promptHtml: Lead the review: root cause and corrected architecture.

sections.label: What a weak answer looks like
sections.html: "Clear the cache" and blame the pricing team.

sections.label: Strong answer
sections.html:
1. Clarifying questions I'd ask: Who owns price? Which store did checkout read? How does each copy get updated (sync, import, CDC)? What compensation is owed to customers?
  2. Immediate mitigation: Freeze CMS imports, reindex search from the pricing source, flush stale price cache, correct or honor the displayed price per policy.
  3. Hypotheses, ranked: No single system of record for price; copies updated by separate paths; no reconciliation; teams own stores independently.
  4. How I'd verify: Diff job across stores for the sale SKUs; trace update timestamps and writers.
  5. Root cause: Four writable copies of one fact; the dual-write via independent paths is the classic drift pattern. Not a "cache problem".
  6. Fix: Name the pricing database as the system of record; derived stores (search, cache, document store view) update only from change events (CDC or outbox), idempotent and versioned; CMS can edit descriptions but not price; the checkout path reads price from the source of truth at order time and stores the price paid on the order. Add a reconciliation job comparing stores with alerts on drift above 0.
  7. Prevention: Data ownership map per field; contract tests; a rebuild runbook for each derived store; display-price vs charge-price check in checkout.
  8. Trade-offs & what I'd NOT do: More stores mean more ways to drift, so each needs a justification; consolidating Mongo into Postgres JSONB could be worth it. Do not rely on cache TTL for correctness.

sections.label: Curveball follow-ups
sections.html:
• CDC lag during a sale? -> Show "price confirmed at checkout"; checkout reads the source.
  • Customer charged more than shown? -> Policy decision; legally risky, fix at checkout with the displayed quote.

sections.label: Senior war story
sections.html: A "price" field appeared in six systems; the cleanup was less about technology than naming one owner.

sections.label: Scoring rubric
sections.html:
• No hire: Flush the cache.
  • Hire: Single source of truth with derived stores via events.
  • Strong hire: Field ownership, reconciliation, checkout reads truth, remediation policy.
